title_content.content: A R T I C L E I N F O

paragraph_content.content: Keywords: Cobalt electrodeposition Suppressor Leveling additive ADO

title_content.content: A B S T R A C T

paragraph_content.content: Adenosine (ADO) was selected as a leveling additive for superconformal cobalt filling in X-shaped through-hole. Changes in deposition potential and the generation of new stripping peaks in cyclic voltammetry curves were observed in electrochemical tests of ADO-containing plating solution. The adsorption behavior of ADO on the cobalt surface was investigated using density functional theory calculations, molecular dynamics (MD) simulation, and electrochemical in situ Fourier transform infrared (E-FTIR) spectroscopy tests. Furthermore, the Co<sup>2+</sup> with ADO coordination was simulated via interaction region indicator analysis. Based on the changes of the ADO adsorption sites from the MD and E-FTIR analyses, an intramolecular synergistic acceleration–suppression mechanism was proposed to explain the effects of low-concentration acceleration but high-concentration suppression in cobalt deposition. Surface analysis revealed that ADO exhibited a grain refinement effect, and crystal analysis showed that the Co hcp (002) crystalline plane was preferentially formed. Finally, X-shaped throughhole with a maximum aspect ratio of 2:1 formed cobalt superconformal filling, with a surface deposition thickness of the cobalt layer as low as 1.2 μm and meanwhile a filling rate ≥90 %.

Electronic interconnect technology is the key for realizing advanced packaging and chip interconnection. With the development of semiconductor technology, the line resistance of copper considerably increases because of the large mean free path of electrons, copper cannot meet the process requirements of damascene filling. However, cobalt exhibits good electrical conductivity and a small mean free path of electrons [1,2], which can prevent electron scattering at the surface interface [3]. In addition, the coefficient of thermal expansion of cobalt (13.3 × 10^-6/K) is similar to that of silicon (10 × 10^-6/K) [4,5], and the internal stresses generated during high-temperature annealing are smaller than those generated during high-temperature annealing of copper [6]. Cobalt is considered the most promising alternative metal for nanoscale interconnect technology.

The bottom-up superfilling phenomenon of cobalt has been increasingly studied, and various micro-nanoscale mechanism models have been proposed. Such models include hydrogen-induced inactivation mechanisms [7,8], voltage-dependent suppression mechanisms [9, 10], S-type negative differential resistance mechanisms [11,12], and differential current efficiency filling mechanisms [13]. Rigsby et al. [12] proposed a differential current efficiency filling mechanism and achieved damascene filling of cobalt. Using the differential current filling mechanism, Ni et al. [14] introduced polyvinylpyrrolidone into electrodeposition of cobalt to achieve a superconformal silicon trench filling. Ma et al. [15,16] used the S-type negative differential resistance mechanism with malachite green and achieved micro blind hole filling of cobalt. Li et al. [17,18] achieved micro blind hole filling with different pore sizes using nitrotetrazolium blue chloride, applicable to S-type negative differential resistance mechanism theory. Huang et al. inves tigated the role of oxime additives and concluded that the amine group can suppress cobalt electrodeposition by coordinating with
19]. In addition, it was proposed that Co
\left( \mathrm { O H } \right) ^ { - }

was the intermediate for cobalt deposition [20], which explained the difference in cobalt deposition rates at different pH levels. Li et al. [21] delved into the efficacy of 5-alkynylpyrimidines as inhibitors for cobalt superfilling by curbing excessive growth in specific regions to ultimately obtain homogeneous and compact cobalt coating. Ni et al. [22] explored the combined effects of 3-mercapto-1-propanesulfonate and polyvinylpyrrolidone on the growth dynamics of cobalt pillars during electroplating and uncovered a synergistic interaction to efficiently modulate the morphology and dimensions of these pillars. Cao et al. [23] conducted the effects of dimethylglyoxime, 3-mercapto-2-propanesulfonate, and histidine on the growth characteristics and magnetic properties of cobalt electrodeposited on copper substrates and discovered notable impacts on the coating morphology, structure, and magnetic attributes. Li et al. [24] focused on the electroplating of nanocrystalline cobalt within sulfate baths with butynediol ethoxylate to produce coatings with exceptional crystallinity and superior surface morphology. Tong et al. [25] examined the role of alkyne-PEG4-amine as an inhibitor in cobalt superfilling, showing its superiority in hindering cobalt growth in select areas to achieve even and dense coating. Wu et al. [26] assessed the performance of phenyl methyl sulfoxide as an additive for cobalt superfilling to significantly enhance the coating uniformity and density and improve the reliability of the three-dimensional interconnect. Furthermore, the design of an in-situ micro-reactor electrochemical experiment is crucia for investigating cobalt valence in complex intermediates and tracking its reduction process effects [27].

paragraph_content.content: Herein, using adenosine (ADO) as an additive with the lowconcentration acceleration but high-concentration suppression and the differential current efficiency filling mechanism during cobalt deposition, superconformal filling of cobalt in X-shaped through-hole was achieved. Through density functional theory (DFT) calculations and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, this electrochemical effect was elucidated in terms of electrostatic potential (ESP) on the molecular surface and the adsorption energy of ADO on the cobalt surface, respectively. The shift in the type of ADO electrochemical action at different concentrations was elucidated in terms of the change in adsorption sites during electrochemical in situ Fourier transform infrared (E-FTIR) spectroscopy tests. Finally, cobalt filling with ultrathin surface deposition thickness (SDT) outside the hole was realized via the low-concentration acceleration but high-concentration suppression effect of ADO.

With an increase in the concentration of ADO, a stripping peak was generated at −0.7 V (Fig. 1c), which differed from the stripping peak position of cobalt [13,32]. It was speculated that ADO could generate complexes with
{ \mathsf { C o } } ^ { 2 + }

and change the deposition-stripping process of cobalt. During the stripping process, the stripping peak was only observed during the first cycle of the CV test, the ADO solution alone did not produce a peak so the effect of the solution was negligible. Thereby confirming that the peak originated from the stripping of cobalt metal under the action of ADO.
As the ADO concentration increased, the process was divided into three phases (Fig. 1d). When the ADO concentration was 5 mg/L, the Q/
Q _ { O }
value was slightly elevated. During the concentration of 10~50 mg/ L, the second stage phenomenon of rapid decrease of
Q / Q _ { O }
value with the addition of ADO could be observed. In the third stage, the
Q / Q _ { O }

values remained relatively stable, illustrating that the ADO in the bath had reached a supersaturated concentration [31]. Above result was approximately the same to the case in Fig. 1a, confirming that the low-concentration acceleration but high-concentration suppression effect of ADO during cobalt deposition. Given that the concentration of 50 mg/L situated close to the intersection of the second and third stages, where ADO had just reached saturation, 50 mg/L was selected as the optimal concentration for DC plating [14,31].

As shown in Fig. 1e of GM test result, the deposition potential of cobalt deposition at high rotational speed, also exhibited a negative potential shift when 10 mg/L ADO was added. However, a large negative shift occurred in the condition of adding 20 mg/L ADO at low rotational speeds. In addition, the potential of cobalt deposition at high rotational speed was more negative than that at low rotational speed, indicating that the suppression of ADO was also dependent on the rotational speed. Nevertheless, when the ADO concentration reached 150 mg/L, the change of deposition potential was reversed during cobalt deposition.

It was observed that ADO exhibited a low-concentration acceleration but high-concentration suppression effect during the electrochemical test. Combined with the results in Fig. 1d and e, in order to avoid the potential reversal phenomenon caused by the concentration, 50 mg/L was selected as the concentration of ADO for DC cobalt plating.

paragraph_content.content: The surface ESP of the ADO molecule was within the range from −50.39 to 56.25 kcal/mol, and the higher surface ESP could result in the stronger electrostatic adsorption on the cathode surface [34,35]. The high ESP region of the ADO molecule was extremely dispersed, and the electrostatic adsorption on the cathode surface was in a multipoint adsorption state. The adsorption sites were –NH<sub>2</sub> of adenine moiety and –OH of nucleoside moiety. A lower ΔE suggested that ADO was more likely to receive and provide electrons on the cathode surface during electrochemical reactions while having a larger adsorption strength in the electric field [36–38]. With no MO distribution on the nucleoside group, so it exhibited only electrostatic adsorption and low adsorption strength on the cobalt surface. Thus, the electrochemical active site of ADO was the adenine group. According to the MO distribution characteristics and the electrochemical test results, it was hypothesized that the nucleoside group accelerates cobalt deposition, the adenine group suppresses cobalt deposition, and the adsorption site of the adenine group increased at a high concentration, rendering the suppression effect dominant [39,40]. However, the reliable correlation between simple HUMO-LUMO calculations and inhibition efficiency was questioned in early work [41]. Therefore, more relevant simulations of IRI and MD simulations were added to further support the explanation of ADO suppressesing function during cobalt electrodeposition.
To investigate the interaction of ADO with
{ \mathsf { C o } } ^ { 2 + }

and the complex structure, the distribution of the weak interactions of the complexes was analyzed by the IRI method [42], and the results of the weak interaction visualization analysis were shown in Fig. 3. The strong interactions were masked in the figure to highlight the distribution of the weak interactions. As shown in Fig. 3b, the distribution of the weak interactions of the complexes was near the adenine moiety, and the introduction of
\mathsf { C o } ^ { 2 + }
resulted in a clear conical interaction zone in the adenine moiety. As shown in Fig. 3c and d, the planar interaction distribution confirmed the enhanced interaction between
{ \mathsf { C o } } ^ { 2 + }

and adenine moiety, suggesting that the formation of a stable structure between them. The stabilized structure confirmed that cobalt bonded with the adenine group in ADO to generate a complex, which explained the generation of the new electrochemical stripping peaks shown in Fig. 1.

All the boundaryless models involved were optimized by the universal force field, and the ADO molecular structure model was built by the Materials Studio software and structurally optimized via the clean force field [43].

paragraph_content.content: With an increase of ADO concentration, the intensity of N–H absorption peaks attributed to adenine groups at 821
\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }
and
1 6 6 4 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }

increased, confirming that the adsorption of adenine groups on the cobalt surface increased. The intensity of the corresponding absorption peaks of the nucleoside groups did not considerably change, indicating that the nucleoside groups could be in the maximal adsorption state. The E-FTIR results indicated that the nucleoside group were preferentially adsorbed, and the adsorption of adenine group was enhanced as the concentration of ADO increased.

Above change could attribute to the ESP distribution of ADO in Fig. 2: the nucleoside group with the largest ESP value preferentially adsorbed but adsorption intensity of adenine group could be improved with the increase of ADO concentration. The E-FTIR test and MD simulation showed that the adsorption of adenine groups increased with an increase in concentration, whereas the nucleoside group was always in the maximum adsorption state. Combined with the electrochemical phenomenon where ADO accelerated the cobalt deposition at a low concentration and suppressed the cobalt deposition at a high concentration, this showed that the nucleoside group accelerated cobalt deposition, and the adenine group suppressed the deposition of cobalt.

During the electrochemical testing, ADO was observed to have a low concentration acceleration but high-concentration suppression effect on cobalt deposition. The electrochemical tests, MD simulations, DFT cal culations, and E-FTIR tests explained the reasons for the acceleration at a low concentration and suppression at a high concentration. First, nucleoside groups accelerated cobalt deposition, whereas adenine groups form complexes with
{ \mathsf { C o } } ^ { 2 + }

to suppress cobalt deposition. Thereafter, adenine groups adsorbed more on the cobalt surface with an increase of the concentration of ADO. Thus, the acceleration disappeared and the suppression increased with an increase of the concentration.

Fig. 6 showed the crystal morphology and contact angle changes in cobalt under different conditions as well as the changes in grain orien tation and the coating roughness data. As shown in Fig. 6a–c, the addition of ADO made the cobalt grains significantly smaller, which had the effect of refining the grains. In addition, the distribution of the grains was more uniform, and the uniformity of the plated layer improved. The addition of ADO significantly reduced the contact angle from 105.6◦ to 61.9◦, and the surface energy increased from
to

. The smaller surface contact angle improved the wettability of the plating solution [52,53], which was conducive to the faster release of hydrogen and the enhancement of the deposition uniformity [54–56]. The change in surface three-dimensional images of roughness tests indicates that ADO significantly improved the quality of the plated layer. The surface roughness decreased from 0.541 to 0.318 μm, and the uniformity of the plated layer improved. The roughness test and the morphological analysis showed that the addition of ADO significantly improved the quality of the plated layer, which was conducive to the reduction of signal transmission loss [57,58].

XRD was performed to analyze the effect of ADO on the crystal orientation (Fig. 6d). Cobalt deposition was achieved on the surface of the copper layer, and a peak of Cu (220) was observed at 74.1◦. The peaks corresponding to the (100), (002), (102), and (110) crystalline

paragraph_content.content: planes of Co hcp were correspondingly observed at 41.7◦, 44.2◦, 47.6◦, and 75.9◦, respectively. The dominant crystalline plane at 0 mg/L con centration was (100); above 10 mg/L, a tendency to suppress the growth of the (110) and (100) crystalline planes and promote the growth of the (002) plane was observed. Although (002) became the dominant crystalline plane at a concentration of 50 mg/L, the intensity of (100) further decreased, and (110) disappeared. The (100) crystal plane of cobalt deposits performed preferential growth when no ADO was added into the plating solution. However, at low concentrations of ADO, the nucleoside group played a significant role in accelerating the growth of the (002) crystal plane. When the ADO concentration increased to 50 mg/L, the growth of the (100), (101), and (110) crystal planes was suppressed instead of the prior growth of (002) crystal plane due to the adenine group for the dominant growth factor. Overall, ADO suppressed the growth of cobalt at (100) and (110), making (002) the dominant crystalline plane. As illustrated in Fig. 6, when the cobalt (002) crystal plane emerges as the predominant orientation, the coating exhibited finer grains, a smoother surface texture, and enhanced hydrophilicity

SEM observations and three-dimensional surface topography demonstrated that the inclusion of ADO led to substantial grain refinement and a notable decrease in surface roughness for electrodeposited cobalt. XRD measurements additionally validated that in the condition of 50 mg/L ADO concentration, the predominant crystalline plane during cobalt deposition transferred to the (002) direction within the hexagonal cobalt crystal lattice.
DC electroplating was performed to corroborate the effect of ADO on cobalt filling. The through-hole filling of cobalt was conducted in a 1.5 L Haring cell with a current density of
0 . 5 ~ \mathrm { A } / \mathrm { d } \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 }

and plated with a DC power supply for 4 h. Cathodic bubbling was employed during the plating process at a bubbling rate of 2.5 L/min. Here, 50 mg/L of ADO was added during plating, and the X-shaped through-hole filling of cobalt was achieved with the SDT value of 1.2 μm. The pH of plating solution was changed nonlinearly during the cobalt deposition because no acidic or basic substances were added to stabilize the pH value. After plating for 1 h, 2 h and 4 h, the pH values of plating solution were observed as 3.2, 2.6 and 2.3, respectively. The rate of cobalt deposition could become slow due to the decrease of pH value [20,59], thereby leading to thin layer of cobalt growth outside the X-shaped through-hole.

As shown in Fig. 7, ADO was mainly concentrated in the region outside the X-shaped holes, which suppressed the cobalt deposition outside the holes. After 1 h of DC plating, cobalt formed a butterfly-type structure in the X-shaped through-hole, at which time the thickness of the deposited layer outside the hole was less than 1 μm. The X-shaped through-hole filling was achieved after 4 h of DC plating, with a filling rate of ≥90 %, and the thickness of the deposited layer outside the hole was only 1.2 μm.

As shown in Fig. 8a, ADO was adsorbed on the surface of the cathode under electrostatic forces. This resulted in preferential adsorption on the electrode surface outside the pore owing to the difference in liquid mobility and low ADO concentration inside the pore. The DFT calculation, MD simulation, and E-FTIR spectroscopy revealed that the adenine group adsorption increased after the ADO concentration increased, thereby showing suppression of
{ \mathsf { C o } } ^ { 2 + }
deposition, confirming that ADO accelerated Co deposition at low concentrations and suppressed cobalt deposition at high concentrations during the electrochemical test. Thus, as shown in Fig. 8b, the
{ \mathrm { C o } } ^ { 2 + }
in the hole was preferentially reduced to
{ \mathsf { C o } } ^ { 0 }

for accelerating the cobalt deposition, and forming a butterfly-type structure. Although the surface of the electrode outside the hole was strongly suppressed by ADO, the cobalt deposition rate was low and the cobalt layer thickness was below 1 μm. As the deposition process advanced, the curvature of the cobalt layer augmented, leading to an improvement in surface mobility and an increased propensity for ADO adsorption, resulting in a higher adsorption concentration, ultimately suppressing the deposition of cobalt within the pore. As shown in Fig. 8c, the deposition rate decreased. Finally, as shown in Fig. 8d, under the low-concentration acceleration but high-concentration suppression ef fect of ADO, superconformal filling was realized.

During the electrochemical test, it was observed that ADO exhibited a low-concentration acceleration but high-concentration suppression effect. By analyzing the HOMO-LUMO and ESP values, discovered that the ADO adsorption sites could be categorized into two distinct groups: adenine and nucleoside. Subsequent MD simulations revealed that the specific adsorption sites were the –OH within the nucleoside group and the –NH within the adenine group. Furthermore, the E-FTIR test indicated that the –OH in nucleoside group were preferentially adsorbed, and as the concentration of ADO increased, the adsorption of the –NH in adenine group was enhanced. These findings were consistent with the ESP calculations, which identified the –OH in nucleoside group as the maximum point and the –NH in adenine group as the sub-maximum point. Combined with the results of electrochemical tests and IRI sim ulations, it is concluded that the nucleoside groups which containing multiple –OH played an accelerating role in cobalt deposition, while the adenine group which coordinated with
\mathsf { C o } ^ { 2 + }

played a role in suppressing cobalt deposition. The difference in the adsorption intensity of nucleoside and adenine groups leads to the low-concentration acceleration but high-concentration suppression effect of ADO in the cobalt electrodeposition.

SEM images and three-dimensional images of plated cobalt showed that ADO had the effects of grain refinement and surface roughness reduction. XRD results showed that under the influence of 50 mg/L ADO, the dominant crystalline plane for cobalt deposition was the (002) crystalline plane in the cobalt hexagonal crystal system. The surface quality of the plated layer improved; moreover, the cobalt grains were refined, and the surface roughness was reduced, which was conducive to the reduction of signal transmission loss.
